title: 5 Reasons Creatine Is Worth a Look After 40
meta_description: What the research says about creatine after 40: muscle creatine stores, lean mass with strength training, why a loading phase is optional, and why daily consistency matters most.
summary: Creatine monohydrate is one of the most-researched supplements in sports nutrition. Here is what the studies found, what they did not test, and the one habit that decides whether it does anything for you.

items.title: It's one of the most-studied supplements in sports nutrition
items.body:
The International Society of Sports Nutrition reviewed the creatine research and concluded that creatine monohydrate raises the creatine stored in muscle and supports high-intensity exercise and lean mass gains during training. The same review found that short- and long-term use appeared safe and well tolerated in healthy people (Kreider et al., 2017).

If you take medication or have a kidney condition, check with your doctor before you start.
items.evidence: Position stand, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2017 (human research review)

items.title: It tops up the creatine stored in your muscles
items.body:
In a classic study of 31 men, muscle creatine rose by about 20% after a six-day high-dose "loading" week. A group taking a small daily amount reached a similar 20% rise more gradually, over 28 days (Hultman et al., 1996).

That study used creatine powder and measured muscle creatine levels, not strength.

chart.title: Muscle creatine: two routes to the same level
chart.source: Hultman et al., J Appl Physiol 1996 (n = 31 men). Bars show the approximate rise reported in the abstract.

items.title: With strength training, it's linked to more lean mass in older adults
items.body:
A meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials with 721 older adults (average ages 57 to 70) found that creatine plus resistance training produced about 1.37 kg more lean mass than training alone, along with greater gains in chest-press and leg-press strength (Chilibeck et al., 2017).

The training mattered: creatine was studied alongside lifting, not instead of it.
items.evidence: Meta-analysis of randomized trials, Open Access J Sports Med 2017
items.alt: An older adult's hands gripping a light dumbbell on a home gym bench

items.title: You don't need a loading phase
items.body: Loading fills muscles faster, but a steady small daily amount gets you to a similar place within a few weeks (Antonio et al., 2021). We compare both approaches in our guide: Creatine gummies loading phase: is it needed?
items.evidence: Research review, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2021

items.title: It only works if you take it every day
items.body:
In the same 1996 study, muscle creatine stayed up while people kept taking a small daily amount. When they stopped, it drifted back to where it started within about 30 days (Hultman et al., 1996).

So the real question isn't which week you start. It's whether you'll still be taking it in month three.

bridge.heading: Convenience is part of consistency
bridge.body:
Creatine is usually sold as a powder: scoop it, mix it, shake it, rinse the bottle. It clumps, it gets gritty, and it's one more thing to pack when you travel. Those small hassles are exactly how a daily habit turns into an every-other-week habit.

If the format is what keeps you from taking it daily, change the format. FusiForce is one option: creatine monohydrate in a chewable gummy, so there's nothing to measure or mix.
